implementation_notes: Kotlin's realization is a structured-concurrency primitive: withTimeout(ms) runs the block as a child coroutine and cancels it with TimeoutCancellationException when the budget expires, withTimeoutOrNull returns null instead, and select { onTimeout { } } reacts to the expiry inline. Cancellation is cooperative - the block must suspend or check isActive, and blocking JVM code has to be wrapped in runInterruptible - and a timeout finishing with a CancellationException is not propagated to the parent scope by design. The hand-written timer is replaced by these operators; the classic form reappears only when the code being bounded is not suspendable.
pitfalls: withTimeout does not stop non-suspending code: Thread.sleep(10_000) inside the block still takes ten seconds, so wrap blocking JVM calls in runInterruptible.
TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so a broad catch (e: CancellationException) swallows the timeout and the caller can no longer tell it apart from an ordinary cancel.
A timeout inside launch{} does not fail the surrounding scope: the CancellationException is not propagated to the parent, so the result must be checked.
The timeout can fire after the block finished but before the caller resumes, so an expiry can be thrown at the await boundary of already-completed work.
